name: Viper oil

lead: Viper oil was a fat-based remedy commonly recommended in 18th-century Europe, especially Britain, for many ailments, and later rattlesnake oil was favoured for rheumatism and skin diseases. Skin conditions are the link to appearance.
Its effectiveness was never thoroughly examined, and much 'snake oil' sold later contained no snake at all.

paras: It was applied as a liniment to the skin in historical practice.
No modern safety data exist. Some late patent medicines contained camphor, turpentine and other ingredients.

chain: Fat from vipers rendered into oil
angle.text: Historically it was used on the skin for skin disease and other complaints; no modern trial tests it.[1]

lead: Viper oil was a remedy made from viper fat, commonly recommended in Europe, especially Britain, for many ailments in the 18th century.[1] People applied it hoping to improve skin conditions; American rattlesnake oil was later preferred for rheumatism and skin diseases.[1]

Its effectiveness was never thoroughly examined.[1] Much Western 'snake oil' probably contained modified mineral oil rather than snake product; a 1916 Bureau of Chemistry test of Clark Stanley's liniment found mineral oil, capsaicin, turpentine and camphor.[1]

paras: The patent medicine trade began in England, with a patent granted for Richard Stoughton's elixir in 1712; the US had no federal drug regulation until 1906.[1] Clark Stanley pleaded no contest and was fined $20.[1]

timeline.event: Bureau of Chemistry tests Clark Stanley's snake oil liniment.[1]
